connector: It’s Marilla. I came home from an Aid meeting this week expecting a fire in the stove and the tea laid, and I found neither. I’ve told that child a hundred times what happens when she lets just anybody in at the back door. I dare say I’ll tell her a hundred more. You’ll read the rest yourself. You won’t believe it either.

guide2.label: Marilla · before you open the book

rwm.label: Marilla · about Read like a Writer

transcripts.welcome: It’s Marilla. Two chapters, and two scrapes, and I was home for only one of them. The question is what Anne learns from her mistakes, and she will tell you herself, at some length. First there’s word work. Find every doing word in the past that breaks the usual rule, and every word that lost its quiet e. Then read. Then tell each chapter short. Shorter than she would.
transcripts.wgrd: The box says the hard part is leaving out the good bits. That child could make a funeral out of a broken teacup, so I know exactly what it means. These two chapters are full of things you’ll want to tell. Most of them you won’t need. Keep why something happened. Let what it looked like go. And if a detail only makes you laugh, it goes first.
transcripts.dol: The top sentence is from the book, I’m sorry to say, and every word of it is true. Look at the two doing words that changed inside themselves, and the one that only took the usual ending. The bottom sentence is two thoughts jammed together with no stop between them. Give each its own. And the girl in it wants her capital, whatever she’s done.
transcripts.guide1: Four pieces of word work. One is a matching game, and one asks you to remember words without any help. Then two where you tap. Tap only what the directions ask for, not everything that looks interesting. Anne does whatever catches her eye, and I’ve seen where that leads. Read the directions twice. Then do exactly that, and nothing more.
transcripts.morphology: Matching today. Two roots and two little front parts, and what each one means. You met the roots before. The front parts are new company. For each one, think of a whole word you already use that has it inside, and say it out loud. Then take that word apart. What’s left over usually tells you what the part means.
transcripts.vocabulary: The same four words as yesterday, and no cards this time. Match each one to its meaning. If you’re not sure, put the word in a sentence about somebody at home. I could think of one for every word on that list, and I’d rather not say who. Don’t guess. Guessing is how a girl ends up believing a stranger at the back door.
transcripts.grammar: One long sentence with more than one past doing word in it. Tap only the ones that don’t take the usual ending. There’s more than one, so don’t stop at the first. Read it slowly, a word at a time, and ask of each one, did this already happen, and how did it change to show it? I’ve no patience for halfway work. Find all of them.
transcripts.spelling: Six words, and each one once ended in a quiet e. In half of them the e stayed, and in half it was dropped. Tap only the ones where it was dropped. Look at the first letter of what was added. That letter decides whether the e is still needed. It’s a plain rule. I like plain rules. They don’t argue back.
transcripts.guide2: There’s a box here about learning from mistakes. I’ve had a front seat for most of hers. The brooch, the Haunted Wood, the cake with the liniment in it. Every one of them happened under my roof. What I want to know is whether she ever learns anything from them, or only finds a new way to be wrong. Read, and judge for yourself.
transcripts.read: One stop, at the end of the first chapter. Think about what that scrape teaches her, about strangers, and about wanting to look different. Then read on into the second. I was away that afternoon, over at Carmody, so I only learned of it afterward. Watch who comes along, and watch what she says to him. I have my own opinion. Form yours.
transcripts.rwm: I wasn’t there to see this, but I can tell you what happened from the sentence alone. A boy jumps into a boat, and his cheeks are red. Three things, and you know he’s angry and he’s leaving. She doesn’t tell you what he thought. She doesn’t need to. When you write yours, pick three things somebody could see, and trust your reader with the rest.
transcripts.guide3: Now the writing. I’ll say what I’d say to Anne. Answer the question that’s asked, not the one you wish had been asked. If it wants what happened, say what happened. If it wants a reason, give one, and show where in the book you found it. Plain answers. You can be as romantic as you like in your own story. Not here.
transcripts.chapter: The first question asks what color her hair really turned and what had to be done about it. I was the one who had to do it, and I’ll say no more. The second asks how she saved herself, and who came along after. The third gives you her own list and asks you to choose one. Use her words. She chose them carefully enough.
transcripts.workshop: Today you cut something. One sentence that wanders off from the scene, even if you’re fond of it. Then move one, to where it does the most good. The last sentence of a scene is the strongest spot. I’ve never seen the use of saying a thing twice, so this suits me. A good story, like a good kitchen, has nothing lying about that doesn’t belong.

a.raw: anne sank to the floor and wept she had ruined her hair
a.fixed: Anne sank to the floor and wept. She had ruined her hair.
a.why: A capital on Anne, a period where the first thought ends, a capital S to start the second sentence, and a period at the end. Sank and wept are both irregular past-tense verbs.

b.raw: marilla cut the green hair off it was the only cure
b.fixed: Marilla cut the green hair off. It was the only cure.
b.why: The same pattern: a capital on Marilla, a period after off, a capital I to start the next sentence, and a period at the end. Cut is irregular too: its past looks just like the present.

scholar.journal-q1: … and say what Anne could have done differently when the peddler came to the door.
scholar.journal-q2: … and say why Anne still refuses to be friends with Gilbert after he helps her.
scholar.journal-q3: … then say whether you think the cure will last, using something Anne does in these chapters.

match.vanity: Vanity is about how a person looks and how much they care about it. Look for the meaning about too much pride in appearance.
match.implicitly: To believe someone implicitly is to believe them without asking a single question. Look for the meaning about trusting completely.
match.epoch: An epoch is a stretch of time people remember afterward. Look for the meaning about a turning point.
match.diligent: A diligent pupil keeps at her work and doesn’t skip the hard parts. Look for the meaning about working hard and carefully.

notes.wgrd: The hard part of summarizing is leaving out the fun details. Keep why something happened, and let go of what it looked like.
vocab: Too much pride in how one looks; caring too much about appearance.
A memorable period of time; a turning point.
Working hard and carefully; not giving up.
notes.wordParts: port means “to carry” (transport, portable, export). tract means “to pull” or “to draw” (attract, distract, extract).
notes.grammar: Irregular past-tense verbs don’t just add -ed. Some change a vowel (sing → sang), some turn into a new word (go → went), and some don’t change at all (put → put).
notes.spelling: After ce or ge, keep the silent e when the suffix starts with a or o, so the c or g stays soft (courageous, manageable). Drop it when the suffix starts with e or i (noticing, changing).
